c1.story:
Every time you tap buy on a trading app, a surprising number of businesses get paid. The app that took your order. The exchange that matched it with a seller somewhere else in the country. The clearing corporation that promised the trade would settle even if the other side vanished. The depository that moved the share into your demat account and will keep a record of it for as long as you hold it. And if you bought a mutual fund instead, a registrar quietly adds your units to a ledger and sends you a statement every month.

That is the capital markets industry: not the people who invest money, but the people who run the plumbing that money flows through. Since 2020 the volume of water through those pipes has exploded, as tens of millions of Indians opened their first demat account during and after the lockdowns. That made this one of the most exciting corners of the market, and one of the most misunderstood.

The misunderstanding is that it is one business. It is four, and they keep very different shares of the same rupee. The exchanges and depositories own the toll. BSE, MCX, CDSL and NSDL each hold a licence from SEBI that few others have, and charge a sliver on everything that passes through. The brokers, Groww and Angel One among them, drive the traffic onto the road and fight dozens of rivals for every customer. The registrars and rating agencies, CAMS, KFintech and CRISIL, keep the books and stamp the bonds, and get paid on assets that grow every year whether markets are noisy or quiet. And the fintech platforms, Paytm and PB Fintech among them, sell payments, insurance and credit through apps, paying heavily for each customer they win.

Same market, same traders, four very different businesses. The licence decides who keeps the money.

Why does this matter? Because the same piece of news hits the four doors differently. A SEBI circular that makes options trading costlier is a dent for an exchange, a body blow for a broker that earns most of its revenue from options traders, and almost irrelevant to a mutual fund registrar. A booming IPO market lifts the depositories and registrars far more than the brokers. Before you read any headline, know which door your company walks through.
c1.read:
There are four tiles here, one per door, and each one reads top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it describe how the money comes in: a tiny fee on every trade and account, a flat fee per order plus interest, a fee linked to assets or issuance, or a commission on each product sold.
  • The tickers are listed companies that mostly sit behind that door; click one to open its stock page. Notice that NSE is missing from the first tile. It is the largest exchange in the country and is still unlisted, a point the kitchen card comes back to.
  • The profit bar is the heart of the tile. Two doors sit at high: the toll owners and the record keepers. Both hold scarce licences and face one or two rivals at most. Brokers sit at medium, because the price war since the discount-broker revolution has squeezed what each order earns. Fintech platforms sit at low, because winning a customer through advertising and cashback is expensive and the regulator can change the rules overnight.
  • The last line is the bet you are making. Look for the word that keeps recurring: the regulator. It appears, directly or by implication, in all four.

Below the tiles, the analogy maps each door onto a highway, and the so-what line gives the punchline: the toll plaza and the registry keep most of the profit, while the taxis and travel agents fight over the rest. When you own a stock in this industry, the first question is how much of its revenue comes from the toll and how much from the taxi rank.

c2.story:
Picture the journey of a single rupee from a saver in Indore to a company in Pune that wants to build a factory. It passes through five stations, and almost every one of them is a business listed on an Indian exchange.

At the first station sit the people with money and the people who want it: households opening demat accounts and starting SIPs, and companies filing for IPOs or issuing bonds. They are the raw material of the whole industry, and they do not belong to it. Their mood, set by market returns and the interest rate, decides how much traffic arrives.

The second station is where the customer is won. This is the broker app on your phone, the mutual fund distributor in a small-town office, the insurance comparison site. Zerodha turned this station upside down in the 2010s by charging a flat fee instead of a percentage; Groww and Angel One followed and pulled tens of millions of first-time investors in. It is the most crowded station, which is why it keeps the thinnest share of the money.

The third and fourth stations are the toll booths. The exchange matches the order, the clearing corporation guarantees it, and the depository records who owns what. These are licensed by SEBI and there are only a handful of each. CDSL, promoted by BSE, holds most of the country's demat accounts by number; NSDL, the older of the two, holds most of the value because institutions park their holdings there.

The fifth station keeps the books. CAMS and KFintech between them maintain the investor records for nearly every mutual fund house in India, and CRISIL rates the bonds that companies sell. This station rarely makes headlines, which suits it fine.

And then there is the elephant. NSE stands at the third station and dominates it, with nearly all the cash and futures business and most of the options business. Because it is not listed, investors who want to own a piece of the toll have had to make do with BSE, MCX and CDSL. That scarcity is a large part of why those three trade at the multiples they do.
c2.read:
Read the diagram in two passes: first the five boxes left to right, then the band row underneath.

The five boxes follow the money from the saver and the issuer on the left to the record room on the right. Under each station's name you get what happens there and who stands there. Watch the names change as you move across: households and companies on the left, apps and advisers next, then the handful of licensed exchanges and depositories, then the two registrars and the rating agencies.

The band row says who holds each station. The first band is grey, because issuers and households are customers, not part of the industry. Every other band is coloured as Indian listed, which is unusual: in most industries at least one station belongs to an importer, a state company or a foreign giant. Here the whole chain from the app to the archive is Indian and mostly listed. The third band carries the extra word NSE, the reminder that the biggest player at that station sits outside the market.

There is no second band row, because no foreign rival stands at any station. Foreign firms matter in this industry as customers, the big trading houses and foreign funds, not as competitors.

Use it like this. When news breaks, place it on a station and trace who pays. A SEBI rule on contract sizes lands on station three and travels left to the brokers within weeks. An IPO boom starts at station one and pays stations four and five, through new demat accounts and registrar mandates, a quarter or two later. The note under the bands, and the so-what line, tell you why ownership of the third station matters so much for valuations.

c3.story:
Here is the uncomfortable fact at the centre of this industry: a large share of its profit comes from people who are losing money.

SEBI has studied retail derivatives traders more than once, and each time the answer was roughly the same. In the study it published in 2024, about nine in ten individual traders in equity futures and options lost money over the period, and the losses were large. Yet those traders paid fees on every trade, to the broker and to the exchange, and they traded a lot. Weekly index options, which expire every week and cost little upfront, became the most popular product in Indian finance. For a few years the toll on that traffic paid for a remarkable share of the whole industry's earnings.

That is why the customer tiles on this card deserve more attention than they usually get. Options traders are the most profitable customer and the most fragile one, because the regulator regards protecting them as part of its job. Long-term investors are the opposite: they trade rarely, but they open demat accounts, start SIPs and apply for IPOs, which pays the depositories and registrars a small, steady fee for years.

Then there are the customers that live on their own clocks. Companies raising money buy listing services, ratings and registrar work, and they come in waves that follow the IPO window. Commodity traders and jewellers hedge gold and silver on MCX, and they trade hardest when bullion swings, which made 2025 a banner year for that exchange. Power distributors and generators buy and sell short-term electricity on the power exchange. Consumers and merchants pay through apps and buy insurance online, and their growth is decided as much by the RBI as by demand.

Options traders pay the most and are protected the hardest. That tension sets the sector's ceiling.

A company selling to many of these tiles is diversified against any one circular. A company selling mostly to the first tile is a leveraged bet on SEBI's patience.
c3.read:
Each of the eight tiles is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is paying.
  • What they buy tells you which door collects the money: options contracts pay exchanges and brokers, demat accounts and SIPs pay depositories and registrars, listings and ratings pay the record keepers, payments and policies pay the fintech platforms.
  • What moves them is your watch list. Notice how often a regulator appears in this line: SEBI's derivatives rules for options traders, RBI's rules for consumers and merchants, market-coupling rules for power buyers.

A useful exercise is to sort the tiles by how they react to a market fall. Options traders often trade more when volatility jumps, at least at first. Long-term investors and IPO issuers retreat, slowly. Commodity hedgers do not care about the Sensex at all; they care about gold and silver. Power buyers care about the summer peak and coal supply. That is four different cycles hiding inside one industry.

Then map the tiles back to the doors on card one. MCX lives almost entirely on the commodity tile. CAMS and KFintech live on the mutual fund tile. CDSL and NSDL span long-term investors, IPO issuers and institutions. Brokers lean hardest on the options tile, which is exactly why the so-what line under the grid says one SEBI circular can move the sector more than a year of market returns.

c4.story:
Most businesses have to make something before they can sell it. An exchange does not. Once the matching engine is built, the data centre is running and the licence is on the wall, an extra trade costs it almost nothing. The thousandth order of the day and the ten millionth go through the same machines, watched by the same staff. The fee on each is nearly pure profit.

That is why the exchanges and depositories in this industry have some of the highest margins of any listed business in India. It is also why their profits are so jumpy. When volumes rise, revenue goes up and costs barely move, so profit grows much faster than revenue. When volumes fall, the same arithmetic runs in reverse. Analysts call this operating leverage; a trader would call it a geared bet on activity.

An exchange is a toll road already built. The next truck pays full fare and costs nothing.

A broker is a different animal. It has to win every customer, often with advertising and referral bonuses, and keep them with a slick app, a call centre and a risk team watching margin positions. It also pays exchange and clearing charges on every trade, and SEBI's uniform fee rule in 2024 took away the volume rebates that big brokers used to pocket on top. So more of each rupee goes out before the broker sees a profit, and more of what remains depends on how many options are traded.

There is a third line that newcomers miss: float. Exchanges earn interest on the margin money parked with their clearing corporations. Brokers used to earn on idle client money and still earn on margin loans to traders who borrow to buy shares. SEBI has tightened the rules on client money since 2023, which turned a quiet, steady income line into a smaller one.

Finally, notice what does not matter. There are no factories, no inventory and almost no receivables. Fees settle daily. Capex is servers and software, not plants. The moat is the licence and the network of participants, which no amount of capital can buy quickly.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, first for an exchange or depository and then for a broker. Read each chart left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar here is not raw material; it is clearing charges, regulatory fees and pass-through costs. For the exchange it takes about an eighth. For the broker it takes a little over a fifth, because the broker pays the exchange's toll on every trade it sends.
  • The opex bar is technology, people and marketing. The exchange spends about a quarter of sales here; the broker closer to two-fifths, the price of acquiring and serving millions of customers.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is tiny in both charts. These are asset-light businesses.
  • The last bar is what is left. The exchange keeps close to six of every ten rupees; the broker keeps a little over a third. That gap is the toll plaza against the taxi, in one picture.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Transaction revenue, market share and people and technology cost all get a yes: the first two are the top line, the third is the fixed cost that creates operating leverage. Interest income on float, depreciation and interest get a sometimes, because they differ by door. Capex and working capital get a no, the clearest sign that this industry is valued on activity, not assets. A useful habit is to read monthly volumes and market share, then apply the leverage yourself before results arrive.

c5.story:
In March 2020, as the market crashed and the country locked down, something odd happened. Millions of Indians, stuck at home with a phone and a salary still arriving, opened their first trading account. Demat accounts, which had grown slowly for two decades, began to multiply. CDSL, long a sleepy utility, became one of the best-performing stocks in the market.

Then came the options craze. Weekly index options let a trader with a small amount of money bet on the market's move over a few days, and they became India's favourite trade. NSE grew into the largest derivatives exchange in the world by number of contracts traded. BSE, a distant second for years, relaunched its Sensex options in 2023, won a meaningful slice of the market and saw its stock rerate many times over.

The peak came in 2024, and it came from the regulator rather than the market. SEBI's study showed most traders were losing money, and from November it acted: one weekly expiry per exchange, bigger contract sizes, upfront collection of option premiums. The budget had already raised the securities transaction tax on derivatives. In mid-2025 SEBI also barred Jane Street, a large foreign trading firm, over its expiry-day trading, which sent another chill through options volumes. Brokers felt the bust first, as active clients fell and revenue per client dropped.

Markets end most cycles slowly. This one was ended by a circular.

Today the arrow sits just past the bottom. But this recovery has a different engine. Options are capped by the rules, so the growth is coming from elsewhere: a busy IPO market, including the listings of NSDL and Groww themselves in 2025; new demat accounts; and wild swings in gold and silver that have sent MCX volumes to records. This is an up-cycle for the toll owners with diversified revenue, and a slower one for brokers whose income still depends on options.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline beside it and the four hands below.

The clock is a circle split into four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, running clockwise from the top. The years under each arc are when this industry last passed through that phase: a long boom from 2020 to 2024, a short peak in 2024, a sharp bust from 2024 into 2025 and a bottom in 2025. Notice how compressed the second half is. The boom took four years; the peak, bust and bottom were squeezed into about eighteen months, because a regulator can end a cycle faster than a market can. The arrow points at early up-cycle, just past the bottom, and the label beside it tells you why it is only early: IPOs and bullion are up, options are capped.

The timeline runs year by year from 2019. Its colours trace the cycle: neutral in 2019, boom through 2023, a neutral 2024 that hides both the peak and the first curbs, bust in 2025, and the latest entry marked as now.

The four hands are what you watch to move the arrow yourself.

  • Options premium traded per day: flat, below its peak. When this turns up, brokers' revenue turns up with it.
  • Active broking clients: recovering slowly, with an up arrow. Fresh retail interest.
  • IPO and fundraising pipeline: busy, up. This pays depositories and registrars.
  • Commodity exchange volumes: at records, up. This is MCX's hand.

Three of four hands point up, and the one that does not is the options hand. That single flat arrow is why the call favours toll owners over taxis.

c6.story:
Most industries have one or two outside forces that set their weather. This one has a weather god: SEBI. More than any interest rate or market index, the regulator's circulars on derivatives have decided the earnings of exchanges and brokers since 2020.

Think about how a rule travels. SEBI floats a consultation paper. Brokers protest, traders grumble on social media, and the stocks start to price it in. A few months later the final circular lands, often with a start date a few weeks out. On that date contract sizes jump, or an expiry disappears, or a margin requirement tightens, and volume on the exchange drops the same month. No other dial on this card works with such a short, sharp lag.

The second dial is volatility, measured by India VIX, the market's fear gauge. Options are a bet on movement, and when the market is jumpy more people want to make that bet, and the bets get bigger. A calm, grinding market is bad news for options volumes even when it is going up. The third is the level of the market itself, which works more slowly: rising prices bring new investors, fill the IPO calendar and lift mutual fund assets, which feed the depositories and registrars.

A calm market that climbs steadily is good for savers and dull for the toll booth.

Then there are the dials that belong to one door. Gold and silver volatility is MCX's private weather, which is why the bullion swings of 2025 were a gift to it. Power demand matters for the power exchange. RBI's rules on payments, cards and digital lending decide the fate of the fintech door, as Paytm learned when its payments bank was shut down in early 2024.

And there is one two-faced dial. Higher short-term rates mean more interest on the margin money exchanges hold, but a higher cost for brokers funding margin loans. Same dial, opposite effects, depending on which side of the float you stand.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches profits. For this industry, notice how many channels run through volume: contract size, volatility, cost per trade. Volume is the top line, so almost every dial is really a volume dial.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways. Three of the nine dials carry red arrows, and all three are rules: SEBI's derivatives rules, the trading tax and RBI's fintech rules. In this industry the regulator is the main source of downside.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Three dots sit on three dials: SEBI's derivatives rules, market volatility and the market level.

The last column shows today's reading where the dial maps to a series we track: India VIX, the Nifty, silver, the money-market rate, the rupee and electricity output. The three rule dials show a dash, because no index measures a regulator's mood. For those, read SEBI's consultation papers and board meeting outcomes; they are public, and they are the real early warning.

The single diamond is short-term interest rates, with one dot: helpful for the exchange's float, costly for the broker's margin book.

Start with the three-dot rows. The so-what line narrows it further: if you track only SEBI circulars and India VIX, you have most of the swing in exchange and broker earnings since 2020. Add silver if you own MCX.

c7.story:
If this industry is a toll road, its bottlenecks are less about traffic jams and more about who gets to set the toll.

The biggest one is structural and slightly awkward to say out loud: too much of the profit comes from one product bought by people who mostly lose money. A large share of exchange and broker revenue rests on retail traders buying index options. SEBI knows it, and has said plainly that it sees heavy retail losses as a problem to fix. So the industry's most profitable activity is also the one its regulator is trying to shrink. That caps how much any investor should pay for options-driven earnings, however strong they look in a given quarter.

The second bottleneck follows from the first. SEBI can change the fee an exchange charges, the size of a contract, the day it expires and the way brokers handle client money, and since 2024 it has pulled every one of those levers. Each time, the change landed on revenue within weeks.

Third, NSE. It holds nearly all the cash and futures business, which means listed BSE can fight only in a few products, mainly index options on its own expiry day. A gain in share can reverse if a rule change shifts the economics of expiries.

The most profitable product in the industry is the one its regulator most wants to shrink.

Then the recurring headline risks. Technology fails, and when it does the whole market notices: NSE halted trading for several hours in February 2021, and MCX's long-delayed move to a new trading platform in 2023 was watched nervously by every commodity trader. Among brokers, the price war that began with flat fees has not stopped; customers can move apps in an afternoon.

The slow one is client money. Since 2023 brokers have had to pass idle client funds to the clearing corporation rather than use them, which removed a quiet income line. And the two-sided one is the fintech licence: RBI's order against Paytm Payments Bank in 2024 hurt Paytm badly, and handed customers to every rival with a clean licence.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck: its name, why it bites and a severity label. The severity label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural means permanent: it caps returns across the whole cycle, so it belongs in the multiple you are willing to pay. Three rows carry it here: options concentration, NSE dominance and the broker price war.
  • Recurring means it comes back: the regulator cutting the toll, and technology outages. These are the headlines that move a single stock for a week or a quarter.
  • Slow means it is working itself through gradually. Client money rules have already removed most of what they will remove.
  • Two-sided cuts both ways. Fintech licence risk can wipe out one company's business line and gift its customers to another.

Notice that no row is labelled cyclical. This industry's bottlenecks do not ease in a good market; most are built into its structure or its regulator.

Read the top two rows together, as the so-what line does. Options concentration and the regulator's power over the toll together cap the upside for anyone reliant on options. The practical test for any company is simple: what share of its revenue comes from options, and how much from listings, depositories, commodities and fund assets? The lower the first share, the less these two rows can hurt it. Then check NSE dominance if you own BSE, and the price war if you own a broker.

c8.story:
In most industries a regulator sets the boundaries and leaves the business to get on with it. In this one, the regulator writes much of the business model.

Start with SEBI, which supervises almost every company on this page: exchanges, depositories, brokers, registrars, rating agencies and advisers. Every product an exchange can offer, every fee it can charge and every practice a broker can follow passes through SEBI's rulebook. Its board meetings are watched by this sector's analysts the way an oil analyst watches OPEC.

The rules of the last two years show how much power that gives it. The derivatives package from November 2024 cut each exchange to one weekly index expiry, raised minimum contract sizes and made brokers collect option premiums upfront. The uniform fee rule, often called true to label, made exchanges charge every broker the same fee, ending the volume rebates that big brokers had quietly booked as income. Expiry days themselves became a regulated item, because the day a contract expires decides which exchange traders flock to. And the securities transaction tax on options went up from October 2024, adding a cost to every trade.

For exchanges and brokers, the next SEBI board meeting can matter more than the next quarter's results.

Outside SEBI, other regulators run their own corners. The power regulator CERC has ordered market coupling, a single price for power across exchanges, which removes the biggest power exchange's liquidity edge; IEX's stock fell sharply on the day the order came in 2025. RBI licenses payment companies and sets card and lending rules, which decide how fast Paytm and SBI Card can grow. IRDAI and AMFI shape the commissions insurance and fund distributors earn, which is the revenue line for PB Fintech and Prudent.

And one item on this rulebook is not a rule at all: NSE's long-awaited IPO, which still needs final clearance. When it comes, investors get a direct way to own the dominant exchange, and BSE loses some of its scarcity value.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status.

The status column tells you how to prioritise, and in this industry it is telling.

  • Always: SEBI itself, RBI on payments and cards, and IRDAI and AMFI on distribution. Permanent fixtures that set the frame for every company.
  • Live: four rows, all of them SEBI or tax rules on trading. The derivatives curbs, the uniform fee rule, the higher trading tax and the expiry-day rules are shaping revenue right now. This is the cluster that took the industry from peak to bust.
  • Coming: CERC market coupling and the NSE IPO. Both threaten an incumbent's edge. Coupling removes a liquidity advantage for the power exchange, and the NSE listing gives investors a cheaper way to own the toll, which may cap the valuations of the listed exchanges.

There is no row marked new, which tells you something too: the big recent changes have already moved from new to live, and the market has had a year to digest them.

The why-you-care column is where to look when a headline lands. If it mentions contract sizes, expiries or fees, it hits exchanges and brokers. If it mentions commissions, it hits the distribution platforms. If it mentions licences or digital lending, it hits fintech. Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces boils down to one question: once money comes in, who gets to keep it? Rivals can start a price war, suppliers can squeeze your costs, customers can squeeze your prices, newcomers can crowd in, and substitutes can make you unnecessary.

Run an exchange or a depository through that test and it passes almost every line. Rivals? There are two stock exchanges that matter, one commodity exchange that dominates its market and two depositories. Suppliers? Technology vendors and cloud providers have little leverage over a licensed near-monopoly. Customers? A trader can choose a broker, but cannot avoid the exchange toll or the depository record. Newcomers? New exchange licences are rare and slow, and even a well-funded entrant needs years to attract liquidity, because traders go where other traders already are. Substitutes? There is no other way to hold a listed share in India than through a depository.

Now run a broker or fintech app through the same test. Rivals are everywhere: dozens of discount brokers, bank brokers, and new apps launched every year with venture money. The suppliers include the exchanges themselves, which charge brokers fees on every trade and which SEBI now makes charge everyone the same. Customers switch apps in an afternoon, often for a nicer interface or a referral bonus. And substitutes are real, as banks and fund houses offer direct investing without a broker in sight.

The exchange is a supplier to the broker. That one relationship explains much of the gap in their margins.

None of this makes brokers bad investments. A broker that wins scale can still earn excellent returns, as the listed leaders have shown. But the business keeps less of each rupee and has to keep earning its place, while the exchange mostly has to keep its licence and its systems running.
c9.read:
The radar chart has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force exerts. So a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: exchanges and depositories, and brokers and fintech platforms. Look at the overall size first. The exchange shape is a small, perfectly even pentagon, a score of one on every spoke. That evenness is rare: it means no single force threatens the business, just a little pressure from every side.

The broker shape is far larger. It reaches the maximum on rivalry, close to it on buyer power and new entrants, and sits at two on substitutes. Only on suppliers does it come anywhere near the exchange shape, and even there it reaches further, because the exchange is one of the broker's suppliers.

Then look for spokes where the shapes cross. There are none. The broker shape encloses the exchange shape completely, the picture of two businesses in the same chain with a clear pecking order.

The table beside the chart gives the score behind each spoke, from zero for no pressure to three for heavy pressure, with a one-line reason. The reasons are the useful part. If you own a broker that has built a loyal base and a lending book, you might score its buyer power lower; if you own BSE, you might push its rivalry score up, because NSE is a formidable neighbour. Redrawing a shape for a single company is exactly how a good analyst uses this framework.

c10.story:
The beauty of this industry for an analyst is that much of its revenue is published before the company reports it. Exchanges release volumes every day. Depositories release account numbers every month. NSE publishes active clients by broker. If an exchange's quarterly results surprise you, you were not reading the data.

Start with the options premium traded per day. Exchanges now charge on premium rather than on notional value, so this is the real revenue base for both exchanges and brokers. Next to it sits market share by product: options share can shift between exchanges in months, as BSE showed after relaunching its Sensex contracts, and can shift back just as fast if the economics of expiry days change.

Then the customer numbers. New demat accounts tell you whether fresh retail interest is arriving; active clients tell you whether it is staying. A broker can add millions of accounts that never trade, so the active count is the honest one. Revenue per active client tells you whether each customer is getting more or less valuable as fee rules change.

If an exchange's results surprise you, you were not reading the daily data.

Finally, the four numbers that come from the filings. Operating margin and employee cost to revenue show operating leverage at work: in a good year the margin climbs while costs stand still. Revenue growth is volume times price in one line. And net margin is what shareholders keep after tax and the contributions exchanges make to their settlement guarantee funds.

Read them in this order, daily data first and filings last, and the results call becomes confirmation rather than news. The one thing the data cannot tell you in advance is what SEBI will do next, which is why the regulator gets its own cards on this page.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of every company you own in this industry.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, the only column on the page that carries figures. Notice that several rows give two benchmarks, one for exchanges and depositories and a lower one for brokers. That split is the five forces card turned into numbers.
  • Today's industry median is filled in for the last four rows, the ones we can compute from listed companies' annual filings: operating margin, employee cost, revenue growth and net margin. The first four rows, options premium, market share, demat and active clients and revenue per client, come from exchange and depository releases rather than filings, so they show a dash; read them from the daily and monthly data.

One caution matters here more than in most industries. The median blends very different businesses: high-margin exchanges, middling brokers and fintech platforms that have only recently turned profitable. So a median margin will sit below the exchange benchmark and may sit closer to the broker one. Compare each company with the benchmark for its own door, not with the blended median.

The trick is to read three things for any company: its own number, the median and the good mark for its door. An exchange holding its margin while volumes dip, or a broker growing revenue per client despite the fee rules, is the one coming out of the cycle stronger.

c11.story:
Most industries make you guess. This one leaves its fingerprints everywhere, in public, every day. That changes what cross-intelligence means here: the challenge is not finding early signals but knowing which of the many on offer actually lead.

Look at the dots and you will see that most sit at the same quarter. Exchange volumes, new demat accounts, India VIX and bullion swings all tell you about this quarter's revenue while it is happening. They are not forecasts; they are the results, published early. Useful, but anyone can read them.

The genuine early warnings are fewer. SEBI's consultation papers are the most important: a paper published today tends to become a circular next quarter and a volume cut after that. Mutual fund assets and folio counts lead registrar revenue by about a quarter. And draft IPO filings with SEBI speak furthest ahead, about two quarters, because a company that files today lists, opens registrar work and draws new demat accounts some months later.

Put the signals together and you get the three-sign rule. The industry is in a full up-cycle when options premium is rising, demat accounts and active clients are growing, and SEBI is not tightening further. Today two of the three are ticking. Accounts are growing on the back of IPOs, and the regulator has not announced new curbs. The missing sign is options premium, which has stabilised below its peak.

When the recovery skips options, own the tolls that do not depend on them.

That is the shape of an early recovery without options, and it is why the call prefers toll owners with diversified revenue, depositories, MCX and registrars, over brokers and fintech platforms still leaning on options or on the regulator's goodwill. It also tells you what to watch: the day options premium turns up for real, the brokers become the more geared way to play the cycle.

The chart places each outside signal along a line by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel through which it reaches this industry's earnings.

For this industry the picture is lopsided. Four of the seven dots crowd the far left, at the same quarter: daily exchange volumes, monthly demat data, India VIX and gold and silver volatility. Two sit one quarter ahead: SEBI consultation papers and mutual fund assets. One sits two quarters ahead: IPO filings with SEBI. Nothing reaches three quarters. This is an industry with excellent real-time data and short warning periods.

Use the chart as a reading order. Each quarter, start on the right with the IPO filings, then check SEBI's papers and fund assets, then confirm with the daily volume data on the left.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means it is off, and the short note gives today's state. Today there is a cross on options premium, stabilised below the peak, and ticks on demat and active clients and on no further SEBI tightening. Two of three, which the rule calls early recovery.

The call box then gives the view, the points behind it and what would change it: a fresh SEBI curb or tax hike, a deep market fall that dries up IPOs, or bullion calming down. Treat those three as alerts. If one appears in the news, the call is due for a rethink.
